02 Anatomy of Waste

Not all waste is equal.

Before designing anything, the categories had to be made legible. Each type has a different cause, a different cost, and a very different best-case outcome.

Throw Away34%
Damage24%
Shop Worn18%
CVP15%

Throw Away

Pure landfill loss — products that expired or entirely spoiled before anyone could act. This is the category the entire dashboard was built to shrink, because every dollar here is unrecoverable.

Worst outcome · fully unrecoverable
03 Who It's For

Two people, one shared blind spot.

The dashboard had to serve the person on the floor and the person watching the whole region — both drowning in numbers, neither able to find the story inside them.

CM

Charles Miner
Objectives
  • Increase sales while reducing waste
  • Keep the waste-to-sales ratio to a minimum
  • Route as much to CVP as possible and reduce the other categories
Frustrations
  • No clear idea what's happening at the store
  • Hard to determine the causes of waste
  • Difficult to prioritise where to act first
DS
Secondary · Business Lead
David Smirnoff
Objectives
  • Make sure every store meets its target
  • Reduce waste while increasing sales
  • Increase the CVP share of total waste generated
Frustrations
  • No consistent way to benchmark stores
  • Can't see which locations need help most
  • Targets feel abstract without a clear path

06 Exploration

Two phases. One roadmap.

Following an agile method we chose a phased approach. Phase 1 fixes the current experience so it's usable today; Phase 2 builds the intelligence layer on top of it — surfacing drivers, setting goals, and recommending the next action.

Phase 1 · Fix the experience

Improve the current dashboard

Make the current tool usable without changing what it fundamentally is.

1
Clear clutter & improve data viz
2
Drill-down experience
3
Classify and highlight information for better analysis
4
Help identify the gap manually
Phase 2 · Intelligence layer

A dashboard that takes action

Build on Phase 1 so the tool does the analysis and points to the next step.

1
Identify & report key drivers & barriers
2
Analyse, set goals & surface opportunities
3
Alert system for what needs attention
4
Gives next best action proactively
07 Design Principles

Five rules that drove action.

The lens every decision was tested against — from the headline number down to a single item on a shelf.

01

Lead with the answer

Open the dashboard and immediately see where waste is worst and what it's costing. The headline does the work — no hunting, no maths.

02

Insight, then action

Every surfaced problem carries a suggested next step and a potential saving. Data becomes a to-do list, not a report to decode.

03

Let people drill down

From market → store → department → fineline → item. A clear path from the big number to the exact cause behind it.

04

Set goals & track progress

Targets, store rank and a leaderboard turn abstract reduction into something a team can aim at — and feel good about hitting.

05

Reduce clutter ruthlessly

Show the few things that matter now; keep everything else one tap away. Signal over volume, at every level.

08 The Design Outcome

An intelligent store overview.

The new home screen opens on what matters: the store's goal performance, sales, waste and CVP — then surfaces the biggest saving opportunities. Then we added the intelligence layer showing the suggested action and potential dollar savings.
